That removes one of the arguments for counter-clockwise, because the cut is easier taken as a descent toward Mae Chaem, which is the clockwise... no: the cut is ridden Khun Yuam to Mae Chaem going *counter*-clockwise only if you have already come down 108. Read the leg page.

**Flowers, November.** Doi Mae U-Kho above Khun Yuam turns yellow with *Tithonia diversifolia* for a few weeks in November, and Khun Yuam sits on the southern leg. Clockwise puts Khun Yuam on day three or four, counter-clockwise on day two. If the bloom is the reason for the trip, go the way that reaches Khun Yuam on a morning.

**Mist, November to January.** The sea of mist off Doi Kong Mu and at Pang Ung is a dawn phenomenon, so it requires sleeping in Mae Hong Son and getting up. Both directions can deliver that; what matters is that Mae Hong Son gets two nights, not one.

Provenance: inference
Sources: s:open-meteo-aq, s:wp-tithonia-diversifolia, s:wp-monsoon, s:mhs-measured
NEEDS VERIFICATION

## The smoke (story/the-smoke)
Thai: ควันไฟ

### what
From late February the hills burn — crop residue, forest undergrowth, land clearance, on both sides of the border — and the smoke settles into exactly the valleys this road runs through. It lifts with the first rains. This page carries four years of daily figures for every town on the circuit, and says plainly where those figures are weaker than they look.

### story
Two sources were fetched, and they are printed together because they disagree.

**The long record** is Copernicus CAMS through the Open-Meteo air quality service: hourly PM2.5 at ten points around the loop from 1 August 2022 to the day of the build. That is 15,050 point-days. Reduced to a daily mean and then to a month, the shape is not subtle. Take Pai: a July mean of 3.0 micrograms per cubic metre, a December mean of 9.9, a March mean of 26.1, an April mean of 29.8. Thirty of the thirty April days measured sat above 35.4 µg/m³, the figure the United States uses as its 24-hour standard. In July, across four years, not one day did.

The same shape repeats at every point on the circuit, and one thing about it is worth saying out loud: **Chiang Mai is worse than the loop.** Chiang Mai's March mean is 37.8 µg/m³ against Mae Hong Son's 29.1 and Pai's 26.1. The city you leave from is the dirtiest air on the route.

**Where the long record fails.** In 15,050 point-days the model never once produced a daily mean above 99.4 µg/m³. Ground stations in northern Thailand have recorded far higher. A model cell is tens of kilometres across; a Mae Hong Son valley on a windless March morning is not, and the averaging that makes a continental model tractable is exactly the averaging that removes the worst hour of the worst day. *Inference —* read the monthly shape from this data and do not read the ceiling from it.

**The ground record**, such as it is. Thailand's Pollution Control Department runs a national network and publishes the current hour. Its historical endpoint returned 404 on the fetch date, so what this site can show from it is now, not then. And there is a second problem, which is a finding in itself: **Mae Hong Son province — 12,765 square kilometres, the largest by area in the north — has one station.** It is 58t, in Mae Hong Son town. Pai has none. Soppong has none. Khun Yuam, Mae La Noi and Mae Sariang have none. Nobody official is measuring the air in the town most riders sleep in on night one.

### how
The practical version. **February is not the problem** up-country: Pai's February mean is 15.0 µg/m³ and no February day in four years cleared 35.4 there. **March and April are.** **May is over** — Pai drops to 10.0 and stays down. If the dates are fixed and they land in March, the ride is still rideable; what changes is that a viewpoint is a white wall, a long descent is done with stinging eyes, and anyone with asthma is having a bad week. A fitted FFP2 or N95 under the helmet is the mitigation people use; a surgical mask and a buff are not filtering PM2.5.

### today
*Inference —* the scheduling advice this data supports reverses the usual one. The cool season is sold as the season, and November to February is genuinely lovely. But the cleanest air on this circuit by a wide margin is **the rains** — Pai at 3.0 µg/m³ in July against 26.1 in March — and the hills are green, the waterfalls are running and the rooms are cheap. What you trade is dry tarmac.

Provenance: harvested · s:open-meteo-aq
Sources: s:open-meteo-aq, s:air4thai, s:epa-pm25-2024, s:wp-southeast-asian-haze, s:wp-mae-hong-son-province

## Every bike goes up there (story/which-bike)
Thai: รถทุกแบบขึ้นไปได้

### what
Six kinds of machine ride this circuit in numbers. None of them is the wrong answer. What changes between them is which single thing you have to plan around.

### story
**The one thing each bike makes you plan around.**

On a **110–160 automatic**, it is the brakes. A twist-and-go gives almost no engine braking, so on a road measured at four curves a kilometre the brake does all the work for ten kilometres at a stretch. Plan descents in stages with a stop to let them cool. Everything else about the bike is an advantage here.

On a **geared 125**, nothing much. Second gear holds the bike down a hairpin descent on the engine, the weight is nothing, every mechanic on the circuit has the parts, and it climbs steadily. *Inference —* if a single machine had to be named as the best fit for this specific road, the argument for the geared underbone is the hardest one to beat, and it is the cheapest thing in the shop.

On a **250–450 trail bike**, it is the highway. The suspension and the 21-inch front make broken edges and the 1263 a non-issue; what you pay for it is a buzzy, tiring hour on the four-lane section of Route 108.

On a **400–700 twin**, it is the driveway. Real brakes, real engine braking, enough power for the long straights — and 200 kilograms that needs two people to pick up on a wet concrete ramp where the second person may be an hour away.

On a **700cc-plus adventure bike**, it is fatigue. Nothing here is beyond the machine. But a steering input every few seconds for six hours is pleasure at 150 kilograms and work at 250, and the mistakes on this road are made in the last hour of a long day.

**On the back**, it is everything at once — longer stopping, higher weight behind the axle, and a passenger who cannot see the surface coming. Plan about two-thirds the distance.

**What does not change.** *Inference —* the circuit does not sort riders by engine size. It sorts them by whether they know what their own brakes do on the eleventh kilometre of a descent, and that is a question you can answer in one day on the Samoeng loop before committing to four.

### today
The measured numbers that sit under all of this: Route 1095 runs 4.03 curves a kilometre over 185 km, Route 1263 runs 4.25, and Route 1096 runs 4.46. Those densities are what a wrist, a brake and a transmission are each being asked to absorb, and they are the same for everybody.

Provenance: inference
Sources: s:mhs-measured, s:wp-motorcycle-safety, s:wp-scooter-motorcycle, s:wp-underbone, s:wp-dual-sport-motorcycle, s:wp-honda-500-twins

## Clockwise or counter-clockwise (story/which-way-round)
Thai: ตามเข็มหรือทวนเข็ม

### what
Clockwise means north first: Chiang Mai up Route 107 and 1095 to Pai, on to Mae Hong Son, then south on 108 and home. Counter-clockwise reverses it — down 108 to Hot and Mae Sariang, up to Mae Hong Son, and back over the curve road last. Both are 600-odd kilometres. They are not the same ride.

### story
**The case for clockwise.** You hit the hardest riding on day one, fresh, on a light bike, before the panniers have settled and before four days of hills have taken your forearms. Day one is short — Chiang Mai to Pai is the least distance of any leg — so a slow, cautious first afternoon costs nothing. Pai is a soft landing with food and a mechanic. And the long, straight, fast southern run on Route 108 comes at the end, when you want to be pointing at home rather than at a hairpin.

**The case for counter-clockwise.** The first day is Route 108 to Mae Sariang: wide, sealed, four to six lanes as far as Hot, and 265 kilometres of two-lane after it that never asks anything sudden. That is a long, cheap day for bedding in a rented bike, finding out what the brakes do, and discovering the rear tyre is ten years old while you are still near a town that can change it. You arrive at the curve road knowing the machine. Mae Hong Son comes on night two or three rather than night three or four, which matters if you want a morning there.

**Where they actually differ.** Clockwise puts your hardest descent — 1095 dropping into the Pai valley — early. Counter-clockwise puts it last, on tired arms, and on Route 1095 tired arms are a real argument. Against that: counter-clockwise gets the rental bike's unknowns out of the way on the forgiving road, which is the same argument pointed the other way.

*Inference —* the disagreement survives because both sides are right about different riders. A confident rider on a familiar bike should go clockwise and enjoy day one. A rider collecting an unknown rental should go counter-clockwise and spend day one finding out what they have got.

**And then the season changes the answer,** which is the part the bar argument usually misses. See the grid on /which-way/.

Provenance: inference
Sources: s:thwp-108, s:doh-1095, s:mhs-measured, s:osm

## The 1,864 sign (art/the-1864-sign)
Thai: ป้าย 1,864 โค้ง

### what
The roadside sign, and the shirts, mugs and stickers that carry the same figure through Pai.

### story
*Inference —* the interesting thing about this object is that it is doing a job no survey asked it to do. Nobody publishes a method behind 1,864, no agency claims it, and Thai Wikipedia's own article on the road gives a different figure entirely — *กว่า 2,000 โค้ง*, more than two thousand.

Counted off the OpenStreetMap trace, the Mae Malai to Pai span carries 395 curves at a 25-degree threshold and 450 at 15. For 1,864 to be right over that 94.5 kilometres there would have to be a curve every 51.9 metres.

None of which makes the sign wrong, because the sign is not making a measurement. It is making a promise about what the road is like, and on that it is accurate.

Provenance: cited · s:thwp-1095
Sources: s:thwp-1095, s:mhs-measured, s:osm
